title: A Unified Evaluation Framework of Physical Adversarial Robustness in the Edge VLM Era

problem.summary: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable end-to-end visual grounding via language prompts and generative decoding, demonstrating largely improved zero-shot and open-vocabulary detection capabilities.
statements: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable end-to-end visual grounding via language prompts and generative decoding, demonstrating largely improved zero-shot and open-vocabulary detection capabilities.
As a result, VLMs are rapidly being deployed at the edge in safety-critical real-world systems.

However, the physical adversarial robustness of edge VLMs has not been systematically studied, and the fundamental differences in output with modern object detectors create methodological challenges for fair evaluation.

2.1 Object detection and grounding VLMs Traditional object detectors [12, 27] have centered on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for their superior capability for edge-device deployment due to low inference latency and excellent energy efficiency.

solution.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are transitioning from describing a scene to localizing within one.

components: Given a natural-language reference to an object, a VLM returns a bounding box.

In embodied and autonomous settings [5, 29], a planner then conditions on that box directly [9], with no confidence score to threshold and no signal of uncertainty, so a correct box and an incorrect one arrive in the same form.
Recent grounding VLMs are increasingly built for real-world deployment, with compact sub-4B variants suited to embedded accelerators [43, 30, 39, 4, 20].

limitations.summary: Under one attack framework, one occlusion control, and a single shared predicate, edge grounding VLMs can be as vulnerable as the classic detectors, yet they do not fail in the same way: the form of each failure is largely associated with the model's output format rather than its architecture family.
items: Under one attack framework, one occlusion control, and a single shared predicate, edge grounding VLMs can be as vulnerable as the classic detectors, yet they do not fail in the same way: the form of each failure is largely associated with the model's output format rather than its architecture family.
Only the first is visible to a downstream system, while the second may be indistinguishable from a correct detection.
Any grounding model bound for deployment should therefore be evaluated on two axes: how often it fails under physical attack, and whether those failures are visible in its output.
